title: Hydrochemical Evolution and Recharge Characteristics of a Multilayer Groundwater System
content:
Shallow and intermediate–deep groundwaters show clear vertical hydrogeochemical differentiation but retain localized continuity. Recharge pathways, water–rock interaction, and solute transport jointly control groundwater evolution in the multilayer aquifer system.


ABSTRACT

This study investigated hydrochemical evolution, recharge characteristics, and vertical relationships between shallow groundwater (SGW) and intermediate–deep groundwater (IGW). A total of 34 groundwater samples were collected from urban Zhengzhou and analyzed using major-ion chemistry, stable H–O isotopes, principal component analysis, and hierarchical clustering. SGW generally showed higher TDS, Mg2+, HCO3 −, and SO4 2− and greater hydrochemical variability, whereas most IGW samples were less mineralized. Both groups were dominated by HCO3–Ca and HCO3–Ca·Mg facies, with mineral dissolution and water–rock interaction as the main geochemical controls. Stable isotopes indicated a predominantly meteoric origin but contrasting recharge responses: SGW was relatively enriched and more influenced by local recharge, whereas IGW was relatively depleted, consistent with a possible contribution from lateral groundwater recharge originating in mountainous areas. Multivariate analyses further revealed an overall pattern of vertical differentiation with localized hydrogeochemical continuity, indicating that regional differentiation coexists with localized cross-layer similarities within the multilayer groundwater system. Elevated NO3 − in the sampled IGW further indicated that nitrogen influence was not restricted to shallow groundwater.
